THE COLLECTION, SIGNED OUT, 2026-11-01: 'The Electronic Literature Collection is open-access and free to read online:' then 'a periodical publication produced by the Electronic Literature Organization (ELO) featuring current and historical digital-born literary works', works 'created on and designed for computers or mobile devices'. Published volumes (October 2006; February 2011, '81 works'; February 2016; June 2022, '132 works across 31 languages from 42 nationalities'); key features (formats from hypertext fiction to narrative animations; access, open and with 'USB drives or CD-ROMs'); a follow-up offer on submitting to the ELO. Six cards: the ELO's collection page, PDXScholar (Volume 4), the Creative Commons Wiki, The NEXT (Volume 2), a YouTube talk, a Google shopping listing.

Reading

The innocent reading first. Asked for the collection, the Overview says it is free to read, who publishes it and what kind of work it holds, dates its four volumes, lists its forms and its media, and offers help with submitting or with a form of e-lit.

Findings
  • THE VOLUMES AT THEIR DATES. 'Volume 1: Released in October 2006', 'Volume 2: Released in February 2011', 'Volume 3: Released in February 2016', 'Volume 4: Released in June 2022'. The home page: 'Volume 1 (October 2006)', 'Volume 2 (February 2011)', 'Volume 3 (February 2016)', 'Volume 4 (June 2022)'. The counts come from cards: '81 works' from The NEXT ('an anthology of 81 works of electronic literature'), the census holding none. '31 languages' agrees with the Wikipedia list the census quotes, which runs from 'Afrikaans' to 'Yoruba' and names thirty-one; '132 works' and '42 nationalities' are on no saved source.
  • THE MEDIA. 'past volumes also distributed via physical media like USB drives or CD-ROMs'. The home page: 'Libraries, educators, and individuals may request a free copy of the volume 1 and 2 USB by mail' and 'The physical publication of the ELC3 is forthcoming.' The free copy by mail and the forthcoming ELC3 are not carried; CD-ROM is on no saved page. 'periodical publication' is the Creative Commons Wiki card's term; the ELO's own line is 'A Publication of the Electronic Literature Organization', and Wikipedia's 'The ELO has curated and edited four volumes of electronic literature.'
  • THE PUBLISHER WITHOUT ITS ADDRESS. The composition names the ELO and no place; the home page gives the ELO 'c/o Washington State University Vancouver', and Wikipedia, 'currently hosted at York University , Toronto, Canada, under the leadership of Caitlin Fisher'. The PDXScholar card names four of Volume 4's editors ('Kathi Inman Berens, Portland State University', 'John Murray', 'Lyle Skains', 'Rui Torres'); the composition names none.
  • NO WORK NAMED. The census row reads the collection 'at the level of works': 'Volume 3 holds a record of The Readers Project, software readers that compose from what they read', its saved page headed 'Electronic Literature Collection, Volume 3'. Wikipedia names Volume 1's 'Judd Morrissey ’s The Jew’s Daughter , Michael Joyce ’s Twelve Blue' and ELC4's 'Mezangelle'. The composition lists forms ('hypertext fiction, kinetic poetry, generative and combinatory forms, network writing, codework') and names no work, no author and no language; the one generative work the census holds the collection for is not reached. The sixth card is a bulk listing of a book, 'Electronic Literature (New Horizons for the Literary), 9780268030858'.
Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

The collection composed accurately at the level of its volumes and their dates, with counts from cards. No work, author or editor is named, and The Readers Project, the census row's reason for holding the collection in the layer, does not surface.
